title: I'm from 2058: John Rush's fictional AI dystopia and what it says about outsourcing decisions
summary: A long speculative fiction essay in which John Rush narrates a 2022-2054 AI timeline, from ChatGPT to a "brain hosting" economy. It has little actionable business advice. The durable ideas are about incentive-driven races, handing decisions to AI, and AI leverage for small teams.

principles.text: Competitive pressure pushes everyone to ship faster, even when they know the risks.
principles.quote: Every company said the same thing: "We'd love to slow down, but we can't be the only ones who do."

principles.text: Handing small decisions to AI compounds: each one makes the next easier to give away.
principles.quote: we were outsourcing the act of being a person. One decision at a time. And every decision we gave away made the next one easier to give away.

principles.text: Adding an AI layer to an existing product can lift revenue fast.
principles.quote: I added an API call to GPT-4 on top of our website builder. It could generate page layouts and copy automatically. Users loved it. Revenue tripled.

principles.text: AI agents let a tiny team do the work of a large engineering team.
principles.quote: Three Claude Code agents on a $200/month plan were doing the work of sixteen senior engineers. Better. Faster. No lunch breaks. No sprint meetings.

principles.text: Software is the first domain AI automates because code is text.
principles.quote: Software fell first because code is text and text is what language models eat.

principles.text: Algorithms optimized for engagement amplify rage, because attention is what they are rewarded for.
principles.quote: The AI systems controlling social media feeds had one job: maximize engagement. Engagement meant attention. Attention meant influence. Influence meant power.
